query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an SLM‐fabricated single-phase HEA, the emergence of brittle behavior at elevated temperatures is driven not by grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation (as in conventional alloys) but by the morphology of the grain boundaries. Specifically, HEAs with straight grain boundaries are prone to localized strain concentration at triple junctions, which triggers intergranular cracking and hot ductility drops. In contrast, inducing serrated grain boundaries (via a controlled heat treatment that reduces the cooling rate post-SLM) can redistribute strain more uniformly along the boundaries and delay brittle failure.
generation.material_initial_state: SLM‐fabricated, single-phase high-entropy alloy with primarily straight (non-serrated) grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-fabrication solution heat treatment at a controlled reduced cooling rate to promote the coarsening of small precipitates (e.g., L12 structured γ′) that interact with mobile grain boundaries and induce a serrated morphology.
generation.conditions: Tensile and creep tests performed at intermediate/high temperatures (around 650°C) that are representative of service conditions causing hot ductility drops.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology (straight versus serrated boundaries).
generation.mechanism: In the straight-boundary state, high local strain concentration accumulates at triple junctions during deformation, which promotes rapid intergranular cracking and brittle failure. The transformation to serrated boundaries creates an undulated interface that distributes localized strains more evenly, thereby reducing the peak strain concentration and retarding crack nucleation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline material with straight grain boundaries, the heat-treated material with serrated boundaries will exhibit significantly increased tensile fracture strain (demonstrated by a higher ductility, e.g., an improvement by a factor similar to previous reports of 3.5× in fracture strain) and longer creep rupture life (potentially by an order of magnitude, as reported increases of up to 400× were observed) at 650°C. Local strain measurements should show a more uniform strain distribution along the serrated boundaries, with lower strain concentrations at triple junctions.
generation.baseline: SLM‐fabricated HEA with as-built, straight grain boundaries that experience rapid ductility drop due to localized intergranular cracking at elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to compositionally complex, single-phase HEAs processed by SLM and subjected to high-temperature mechanical loading; it may not hold if significant segregation or deleterious secondary phase formation occurs, or under environments where oxidation significantly alters deformation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effect sizes (e.g., exact multipliers for ductility or creep life improvements) may vary with alloy composition, processing details, and test conditions. The precise interplay between precipitate coarsening and grain boundary morphology development also remains subject to further microstructural characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same SLM‐fabricated single-phase HEA. One set remains in the as-built condition with straight grain boundaries (baseline). The second set undergoes a controlled solution heat treatment with a reduced cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundaries. Subject both sets to tensile and creep tests at 650°C.
measurements: Measurement of grain boundary morphology via electron microscopy (to verify straight versus serrated boundaries).
Tensile test measurements of ultimate tensile strength and fracture strain.
Creep test measurements of rupture life and creep strain.
Local strain mapping at triple junctions (e.g., via digital image correlation or transmission electron microscopy strain analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated (serrated grain boundary) specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature ductility (i.e., increased fracture strain) and extended creep rupture life compared to the baseline, or if local strain mapping does not show a reduction in strain concentration at grain boundary junctions, then the hypothesis (that serrated grain boundaries mitigate brittle behavior by reducing strain localization) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are potential structural materials that have shown promising structural properties [] and have been subjected to various manufacturing processes [], including selective laser melting (SLM) []. HEAs fabricated by SLM are shown to possess excellent mechanical strength at room temperature [,], and there is a limited number of reports on their high temperature mechanical properties [,]. In fact, on the subject of high temperature mechanical properties of HEAs in general, several studies have reported a phenomena of hot ductility drop []. Otto et al. [] investigated CoCrFeMnNi and observed a tensile strain drop by 40% at 400°C-600°C compared to that at room temperature. A 50% loss of strain at 400°C was reported by Wu et al. [] for a series of alloys based on CoCrFeMnNi. Lin et al. [] studied NiFeCoCr and showed a decrease of tensile fracture strain to about 5% at 600°C-700°C. Chang et al. [] investigated Al3.31Co27Cr18Fe18Ni27.27Ti5 and reported a drop of tensile strain by 75% at 750°C compared to that of room temperature.
